claim: The human genome encodes approximately 100 putative DUBs.
source: The human genome encodes approximately 100 putative DUBs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as a factual statement about the human genome.

claim: DUBs can be grouped into at least five subfamilies based on the composition in relation to the catalytic motif: USPs, UCHs, OTUs, MJDs, and JAMM domain proteins.
source: Based on the composition in relation to the catalytic motif, DUBs can be grouped into at least five subfamilies as follows: the ubiquitin-specific proteases/ubiquitin-specific processing proteases (USPs), the ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolases (UCHs), the ovarian tumor proteases (OTUs), the Josephin or Machado-Joseph disease protein domain proteases (MJDs), and the Jab1/MPN domain-associated metalloisopeptidase (JAMM) domain proteins (Liu et al., 2018; Nijman et al., 2005)
evidence: This classification is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2018 and Nijman et al., 2005.

claim: siRNAs specifically for USP18, USP41, or USP49 could facilitate Vif-mediated A3G degradation.
source: After two rounds of screening, we identified siRNAs specifically for USP18, USP41, or USP49 that could facilitate Vif-mediated A3G degradation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental screening data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: USP49 was the most capable of inhibiting Vif-mediated A3G degradation among USP18, USP41, and USP49.
source: Among them, USP49 was the most capable of inhibiting this interaction (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the three DUBs shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A3G exerts its antiviral effect in the cytoplasm.
source: Considering A3G exerts its antiviral effect in the cytoplasm (Gallois-Montbrun et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gallois-Montbrun et al., 2007.

claim: USP18 and USP41 were mainly distributed in the cytoplasm.
source: we found that USP18 and USP41 were mainly distributed in the cytoplasm, whereas USP49 was distributed in both the nucleus and cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: USP49 was distributed in both the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: we found that USP18 and USP41 were mainly distributed in the cytoplasm, whereas USP49 was distributed in both the nucleus and cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression of USP41 in primary CD4+T cells was quite low.
source: we examined the expression of these DUBs in natural HIV-1-target cells and found that the expression of USP41 in primary CD4+T cells was quite low (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The expression of USP18 and USP49 in primary CD4+T cells was high.
source: whereas the expression of USP18 and USP49 was high (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and western blotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: USP49 is the most conserved among anthropoids when comparing the sequences of USP18, USP41, and USP49.
source: By comparing the sequences of these DUBs among anthropoids, we found that USP49 is the most conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: USP49 significantly suppressed the downregulation of A3G when Vif levels were moderate.
source: The results showed that USP49 significantly suppressed the downregulation of A3G when Vif levels were moderate.
evidence: This is based on experimental results from dose-dependent transfection experiments.

claim: With an abundance of Vif protein, the protective effect of USP49 was quite limited.
source: However, with an abundance of Vif protein, the protective effect of USP49 was quite limited (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: USP49 counteracts Vif-mediated A3G degradation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, we identified that USP49 counteracts Vif-mediated A3G degradation in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The knockdown of endogenous USP49 could enhance the infectivity of HIV-1 in the presence of Vif.
source: The results showed that the knockdown of endogenous USP49 could enhance the infectivity of HIV-1 in the presence of Vif (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The overexpression of USP49 inhibited HIV-1 infection in a dose-dependent manner.
source: the overexpression USP49 was found to inhibit HIV-1 infection and the inhibitory effect occurred in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Proviral DNAs in cells with a lower infectivity but a higher USP49 dose have more G-to-A hypermutations.
source: The sequencing indicated that proviral DNAs in cells with a lower infectivity but a higher USP49 dose have more G-to-A hypermutations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: USP49 regulated the infectivity of HIV-1 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, USP49 regulated the infectivity of HIV-1 in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: USP49 alone did not have any antiviral effect.
source: We found that USP49 alone did not have any antiviral effect (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: siUSP49 could down-regulate the endogenous A3G and then inhibit HIV-1 infectivity in primary CD4+ T cells.
source: Results showed that siUSP49 could down-regulate the endogenous A3G and then inhibit HIV-1 infectivity (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: USP49 exerts its potent antiviral effect through A3G.
source: Combined with these data, this result indicates that USP49 exerts its potent antiviral effect through A3G.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from multiple experimental results.

claim: Vif-Y40H-mutated HIV-1 viruses exhibited impaired infectivity when used to infect primary CD4+T cells.
source: When Vif-Y40H-mutated HIV-1 viruses were used to infect primary CD4+T cells, their infectivity was impaired (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by P24 ELISA data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In primary CD4+T cells with shRNA-mediated USP49-knockdown, the infectivity of Vif-Y40H-mutated HIV-1 almost returned to wildtype levels.
source: However, in the primary CD4+T cells with shRNA-mediated USP49-knockdown, the infectivity of Vif-Y40H-mutated HIV-1 almost returned to wildtype levels (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by P24 ELISA data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is a lower frequency of G-to-A hypermutation in proviral DNAs in the Y40H mutation control sample compared with suppression of USP49.
source: Meanwhile, compared with suppression of USP49, there is a lower frequency of G-to-A hypermutation in proviral DNAs in the Y40H mutation control sample (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by hypermutation analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The inhibition of USP49 can promote the degradation of A3G and subsequently reduce the hypermutation in virus.
source: This result verifies that the inhibition of USP49 can promote the degradation of A3G and subsequently reduce the hypermutation in virus.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the hypermutation analysis data.

claim: The anti-A3G effect of Vif can be enforced by depletion of the A3G protein stabilizer USP49.
source: These data indicated that the anti-A3G effect of Vif can be enforced by depletion of the A3G protein stabilizer USP49, alternatively supporting the fact that USP49 enhances the anti-HIV-1 effect of A3G.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: In the absence of Vif, USP49 knockdown with siRNA significantly decreased A3G stability.
source: Unexpectedly, in the absence of Vif, USP49 knockdown with siRNA also significantly decreased A3G stability, which could be rescued by MG132 (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: A3G could be degraded through a Vif-independent pathway.
source: suggesting that A3G could be degraded through a Vif-independent pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that A3G degradation occurs even in the absence of Vif.

claim: When DUBs were overexpressed, they promoted A3G protein expression in a dose-dependent manner.
source: When DUBs were overexpressed, they promoted A3G protein expression in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: USP49 enhanced A3G levels in both cell lysates and viral particles.
source: USP49 enhanced A3G levels in both cell lysates and viral particles (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The depletion of endogenous USP49 with USP49-specific siRNA reduced the level of A3G in both ΔVif virus-producing cells and viral particles.
source: Alternatively, the depletion of endogenous USP49 with USP49-specific siRNA also reduced the level of A3G in both ΔVif virus-producing cells and viral particles (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: USP49 stabilizes A3G in both a Vif-dependent and Vif-independent manner.
source: Taken together, we found that USP49 stabilizes A3G in both a Vif-dependent and Vif-independent manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: MG132 blocked the Vif-independent A3G degradation effect.
source: Although MG132 blocked this effect, a NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924, which can inhibit the cullin-RING subtype of ubiquitin ligases, was ineffective (Figure 3F) (Stanley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F and cited reference Stanley et al., 2012.

claim: A NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924, which can inhibit the cullin-RING subtype of ubiquitin ligases, was ineffective in blocking Vif-independent A3G degradation.
source: Although MG132 blocked this effect, a NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924, which can inhibit the cullin-RING subtype of ubiquitin ligases, was ineffective (Figure 3F) (Stanley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F and cited reference Stanley et al., 2012.

claim: siRNAs specific for Cullin1–seven did not affect the Vif-independent A3G degradation process.
source: Further, siRNAs specific for Cullin1–seven did not affect this process (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The cullin-RING subtype of E3 ligases is not involved in Vif-independent A3G degradation.
source: Collectively, although we cannot identify the specific E3 ligase at present, we at least excluded the involvement of the cullin-RING subtype of E3 ligases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data with MLN4924 and cullin siRNAs.

claim: USP49 and A3G colocalize in the cytoplasm.
source: Confocal laser scanning microscopy showed the colocalization of A3G and USP49 in the cytoplasm (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a strong interaction between Flag-USP49 and HA-A3G.
source: We therefore performed a co-immunoprecipitation experiment and found a strong interaction between Flag-USP49 and HA-A3G (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HA-tagged A3G interacted with endogenous USP49.
source: Meanwhile, HA-tagged A3G also interacted with endogenous USP49 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The interaction between A3G and USP49 is direct and not mediated by RNA.
source: We have also performed the experiment with RNase A treatment and found that the interaction between A3G and USP49 is direct and not mediated by RNA (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with RNase A treatment shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Overexpression of USP49 resulted in a significant decrease in the poly-ubiquitination of A3G.
source: As shown in Figure 4E, overexpression of USP49 resulted in a significant decrease in the poly-ubiquitination of A3G
evidence: This is supported by denaturing immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Overexpression of the USP49-C262A mutant, which lost DUB enzymatic activity, failed to alter A3G ubiquitination.
source: whereas overexpression of the USP49-C262A mutant, which lost DUB enzymatic activity, failed to alter A3G ubiquitination (Luo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and cited reference Luo et al., 2017.

claim: The ubiquitination of A3G is regulated by USP49 through K48-linked ubiquitination.
source: As the ubiquitination of A3G depends on the type of K48, we overexpressed K48 ubiquitin and confirmed that the ubiquitination of A3G is regulated by USP49.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with K48 ubiquitin overexpression.

claim: The K48-linked ubiquitination was suppressed when the mutant K48R was used.
source: However, we found that the K48-linked ubiquitination was suppressed when the mutant K48R was used (Figure 4F), which is consistent with previous studies (Mehle et al., 2004; Turner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and cited references Mehle et al., 2004 and Turner et al., 2016.

claim: A positive correlation between USP49 mRNA levels and A3G protein expression was observed in primary CD4+ T cells from newly-diagnosed individuals with HIV-1 infections.
source: As shown in Figure 5, we observed a positive correlation between USP49 mRNA levels and A3G protein expression (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 5A from clinical samples (n=21).

claim: A significant correlation between USP49 expression and CD4 counts was found.
source: Along with the correlation between A3G protein expression and CD4 counts, we also found a significant correlation between USP49 expression and CD4 counts (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 5B and 5C from clinical samples.

claim: A negative correlation between plasma HIV-1 RNA levels and USP49 expression was observed.
source: Conversely, a negative correlation between plasma HIV-1 RNA levels and USP49 expression was observed (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 5D from clinical samples.

claim: No correlation was found between USP18 mRNA expression and A3G, CD4 counts, or viral load.
source: However, we did not find any correlation between USP18 mRNA expression and A3G, CD4 counts, or viral load (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of USP49 in CD4 T-cells of HIV-1 infected individuals could be involved in HIV-1 disease progression.
source: These results suggested that the expression of USP49 in CD4 T-cells of HIV-1 infected individuals could be involved in HIV-1 disease progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the correlation analysis data.

claim: A positive correlation between the percentage of G-to-A mutations and USP49 expression was observed in seven HIV-1-infected individuals receiving suppressive cART.
source: A positive correlation between the percentage of G-to-A mutations and USP49 expression and A3G protein expression was observed in these seven subjects (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6A-D from clinical samples (n=7).

claim: A positive correlation between the percentage of G-to-A mutations and A3G protein expression was observed in seven HIV-1-infected individuals receiving suppressive cART.
source: A positive correlation between the percentage of G-to-A mutations and USP49 expression and A3G protein expression was observed in these seven subjects (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6A-D from clinical samples (n=7).

claim: A significant negative correlation between USP49 mRNA levels and the ratio of intact proviruses was observed in 24 HIV-1-infected individuals receiving suppressive cART.
source: By analyzing 24 clinical samples, we observed a significant negative correlation between USP49 mRNA levels, as well as A3G protein expression, and the ratio of intact proviruses (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is supported by IPDA and correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6F and 6G from clinical samples (n=24).

claim: A significant negative correlation between A3G protein expression and the ratio of intact proviruses was observed in 24 HIV-1-infected individuals receiving suppressive cART.
source: By analyzing 24 clinical samples, we observed a significant negative correlation between USP49 mRNA levels, as well as A3G protein expression, and the ratio of intact proviruses (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is supported by IPDA and correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6F and 6G from clinical samples (n=24).

claim: USP49 contributes to the generation of defective proviruses in the HIV-1 latently-infected cells.
source: Combined with the G to A hypermutation measurements, these data suggest that USP49 contributes to the generation of defective proviruses in the HIV-1 latently-infected cells and therefore the actual size of the viral reservoir.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the clinical correlation data.

claim: USP49 interacts with p53, dual-specificity protein phosphatases (DUSP), or FKBP51 in the nucleus.
source: Recently, it has been shown that USP49 interacts with p53, dual-specificity protein phosphatases (DUSP), or FKBP51 in the nucleus, and consequently suppresses the ubiquitination of these proteins (Luo et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luo et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2018; and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: USP49 can negatively regulate cellular antiviral responses via the deconjugation of K63-linked ubiquitin in STING.
source: Regarding innate immunity, it can negatively regulate cellular antiviral responses via the deconjugation of K63-linked ubiquitin in STING, an adaptor protein that senses cytoplasmic DNA and is involved in various innate immune responses (Ye et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ye et al., 2019.

claim: USP49 stabilizes A3G by counteracting Vif-mediated A3G ubiquitination by removing the ubiquitin from A3G.
source: We also revealed a novel function for USP49 in the cytoplasm; specifically, it stabilizes A3G by counteracting Vif-mediated A3G ubiquitination by removing the ubiquitin from A3G.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: USP49 significantly enhances the anti-HIV-1 activity of A3G.
source: As a result, it significantly enhances the anti-HIV-1 activity of A3G.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: A Vif-independent degradation pathway for A3G exists.
source: By studying the protection of A3G from degradation through DUB knockdown, we unexpectedly found that a Vif-independent degradation pathway for A3G.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations showing A3G degradation in the absence of Vif.

claim: The Vif-independent A3G degradation pathway occurs via the UPS as MG132 could block the degradation and ubiquitination of A3G.
source: This pathway occurs via the UPS as MG132 could also block the degradation and ubiquitination of A3G.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing MG132 blocking A3G degradation.

claim: There are some ubiquitination sites on A3G that are not located at the C-terminus of A3G and not regulated by Vif.
source: This phenomenon could explain why there are some ubiquitination sites on A3G that are not located at the C-terminus of A3G and not regulated by Vif (Albin et al., 2013; Iwatani et al., 2009; Turner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albin et al., 2013; Iwatani et al., 2009; and Turner et al., 2016.

claim: The cullin family is not involved in Vif-independent A3G degradation.
source: At least, we found that the cullin family is not involved, as the inhibitor MLN4924 was ineffective and siRNAs for Cullin1-7 did not affect this process.
evidence: This is based on experimental data with MLN4924 and cullin siRNAs.

claim: The depletion of elonginB and elonginC did not affect the Vif-independent degradation of A3G.
source: Further, the depletion of elonginB and elonginC also did not affect the degradation of A3G, which clearly distinguishes this effect from the Vif-dependent degradation pathway.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: APOBEC proteins counteract many viruses such as hepatitis B virus, adeno-associated virus, and some herpes viruses.
source: It is well known that APOBEC proteins are not only involved in anti-HIV-1 immunity, but also counteract many viruses such as hepatitis B virus, adeno-associated virus, and some herpes viruses (Bulliard et al., 2011; Nakaya et al., 2016; Narvaiza et al., 2009; Suspène et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: APOBEC proteins play a key role in genome stability.
source: They also play a key role in genome stability (Esnault et al., 2005; Narvaiza et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Esnault et al., 2005 and Narvaiza et al., 2012.

claim: APOBEC proteins are involved in the development of mutations in tumors, which is a key factor for tumorigenesis and the development of drug-resistance or the escape from immune surveillance.
source: Especially, they are involved in the development of mutations in tumors, which is a key factor for tumorigenesis and the development of drug-resistance or the escape from immune surveillance (Burns et al., 2013a; Burns et al., 2013b; Law et al., 2016; Swanton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: DUBs prevent the Vif-independent degradation of A3G, showing a new mechanism underlying the regulation of APOBE3 protein expression.
source: We identified that DUBs prevent the Vif-independent degradation of A3G, showing a new mechanism underlying the regulation of APOBE3 protein expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The development of A3G-mediated sub-lethal hypermutations in the Vif-positive HIV-1 genome in vitro and in vivo has been widely accepted.
source: The development of A3G-mediated sub-lethal hypermutations in the Vif-positive HIV-1 genome in vitro and in vivo has been widely accepted (Borzooee et al., 2018; Cuevas et al., 2015; De Pasquale et al., 2013; Jern et al., 2009; Kieffer et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2010; Mulder et al., 2008; Sadler et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A correlation was found between USP49 expression and A3G protein expression in vivo.
source: In this report, we found a correlation between USP49 expression and A3G protein expression in vivo, as well as some important parameters related to HIV-1 disease progression and the components of the viral reservoir, through clinical correlation analysis.
evidence: This is based on clinical correlation analysis data.

claim: The stabilization of A3G protein could lead to sub-lethal hypermutations or eventually lethal hypermutations in the HIV-1 genome, resulting in the accumulation of defective proviruses.
source: Although these data are preliminary, they support the hypothesis that the stabilization of A3G protein could lead to sub-lethal hypermutations or eventually lethal hypermutations in the HIV-1 genome, resulting in the accumulation of defective proviruses.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the clinical data presented.

claim: USP49 and A3G could comprise a strong driving force to contain the actual viral reservoir.
source: Therefore, USP49 and A3G could comprise a strong driving force to contain the actual viral reservoir.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the clinical data.

claim: The expression of USP49 protein in HIV-1-infected individuals could be used to indicate the quality of defective proviruses and the actual size of the viral reservoir.
source: Moreover, our data indicated that the expression of USP49 protein in HIV-1-infected individuals could be used to indicate the quality of defective proviruses and the actual size of the viral reservoir, potentially serving as a possible new biomarker to evaluate the prognosis of HIV-1-infected patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the clinical data.

claim: A3G can be incorporated into vif-deficient HIV-1 virions and mediates C–U conversion in the newly synthesized minus-stranded HIV-1 DNA.
source: It can be incorporated into vif-deficient human immunodeficiency virus type1 (HIV-1) virions and mediates C–U conversion in the newly synthesized minus-stranded HIV-1 DNA to trigger the breakage of viral DNA or the generation of G-to A lethal hypermutations, resulting in a premature stop codon or mutated viral protein (Harris et al., 2003; Mangeat et al., 2003; Sheehy et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A3G can physically block the reverse transcription process.
source: Alternatively, A3G can physically block the reverse transcription process (Bishop et al., 2008; Iwatani et al., 2007; Pollpeter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bishop et al., 2008; Iwatani et al., 2007; and Pollpeter et al., 2018.

claim: A3G exerts potent antiviral activity through combined effects of DNA breakage, hypermutations, and blocking reverse transcription.
source: Because of these combined effects, A3G exerts potent antiviral activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the described mechanisms of A3G action.

claim: A3G induces sub-lethal hypermutations, which would not significantly impair viral infectivity but indicate an important driving force for HIV-1 genetic variations.
source: Meanwhile, it also induces sub-lethal hypermutations, which would not significantly impair viral infectivity but indicate an important driving force for HIV-1 genetic variations.
evidence: This is stated as a known effect of A3G.

claim: Sub-lethal hypermutations ultimately aid in viral evolution or facilitate viral responses to selective pressures such as the development of antiviral drug resistance or the evasion of immune surveillance.
source: This ultimately aids in viral evolution or facilitates viral responses to selective pressures such as the development of antiviral drug resistance or the evasion of immune surveillance (Jern et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2010; Mulder et al., 2008; Sadler et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: HIV-1 Vif can effectively antagonize the antiviral activity of A3G by inducing its degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS).
source: However, the HIV-1 accessory protein viral infectivity factor (Vif) can effectively antagonize the antiviral activity of A3G by inducing its degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) (Kao et al., 2003; Mehle et al., 2004; Sheehy et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kao et al., 2003; Mehle et al., 2004; and Sheehy et al., 2003.

claim: Vif interacts with A3G through its N-terminal domain.
source: Vif interacts with A3G through its N-terminal domain and has a SOCS-box motif within its C-terminal domain, which recruits ElonginB, ElonginC, and Cullin5 to form an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, subsequently mediating the ubiquitination of A3G (Yu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2003.

claim: Vif has a SOCS-box motif within its C-terminal domain, which recruits ElonginB, ElonginC, and Cullin5 to form an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex.
source: Vif interacts with A3G through its N-terminal domain and has a SOCS-box motif within its C-terminal domain, which recruits ElonginB, ElonginC, and Cullin5 to form an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, subsequently mediating the ubiquitination of A3G (Yu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2003.

claim: CBF-β can increase the stability of HIV-1 Vif and promote assembly of the Vif-Cullin 5-E3-ubiquitin-ligase complex.
source: CBF-β can increase the stability of HIV-1 Vif and promote assembly of the Vif-Cullin 5-E3-ubiquitin-ligase complex (Jäger et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jäger et al., 2011 and Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: A3G mediates lethal hypermutations and leads to the accumulation of G-to-A hypermutations in the Vif-positive HIV-1 genome in vivo.
source: Further, some clinical in vivo analyses of Vif-positive HIV-1 quasispecies indicated that A3G mediates lethal hypermutations and leads to the accumulation of G-to-A hypermutations in the Vif-positive HIV-1 genome, subsequently resulting in a large number of defective proviruses in the viral reservoir (Borzooee et al., 2018; Cuevas et al., 2015; De Pasquale et al., 2013; Kieffer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical studies.

claim: The expression level of A3G is correlated with viremia and CD4 counts in the peripheral blood.
source: The expression level of A3G is also correlated with viremia and CD4 counts in the peripheral blood (Amoêdo et al., 2011; Jin et al., 2005; Kourteva et al., 2012; Pace et al., 2006; Ulenga et al., 2008; Vázquez-Pérez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Partial mutations in the vif gene can impair its anti-A3G activity and increase the frequency of hypermutation.
source: Accordingly, partial mutations in the vif gene can impair its anti-A3G activity and increase the frequency of hypermutation (Fourati et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fourati et al., 2010 and Simon et al., 2005.

claim: The UPS comprises the main non-lysosomal intracellular protein degradation pathway that consists of three major components: the proteasome holoenzymes, a number of ubiquitin ligases, and a broad spectrum of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs).
source: The UPS comprises the main non-lysosomal intracellular protein degradation pathway that consists of three major components, the proteasome holoenzymes, a number of ubiquitin ligases, and a broad spectrum of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) (Bailey-Elkin et al., 2017; Ventii and Wilkinson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bailey-Elkin et al., 2017 and Ventii and Wilkinson, 2008.

claim: Ubiquitination is a dynamic and reversible process.
source: Ubiquitination is a dynamic and reversible process, and it has become increasingly apparent that deubiquitination also has an important function in regulating the ubiquitin-dependent pathway.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The roles that deubiquitination play in host–virus relationships are less investigated compared to ubiquitination.
source: However, In contrast to extensive studies on ubiquitination, the roles that deubiquitination play in host–virus relationships are less investigated (Bailey-Elkin et al., 2017; Banks et al., 2003; Nijman et al., 2005; Sowa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Host DUBs play an important role in the maintenance of innate or acquired immunity.
source: In addition to host DUBs, which play an important role in the maintenance of innate or acquired immunity, virus-encoded DUBs also affect the immune system to support their replication (Kumari and Kumar, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kumari and Kumar, 2018.

claim: Virus-encoded DUBs affect the immune system to support viral replication.
source: In addition to host DUBs, which play an important role in the maintenance of innate or acquired immunity, virus-encoded DUBs also affect the immune system to support their replication (Kumari and Kumar, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kumari and Kumar, 2018.
